title: My Review Column
tagline: Opinion writing · Critical thinking · Writing for a reader
goal: Your kid becomes a reviewer. They try real things from their own life, decide what they really think, and write reviews good enough to help someone else choose. The reviews go into their own column, with a name and a rating system they invent.
create: 3 to 5 written reviews of real things they've tried
A rating system they designed themselves
Their own review column, with a name, that someone else can use to decide
need: Things to review: anything your kid already eats, reads, plays or visits
A notebook or folder just for the column
For the taste test: 3 snacks, cereals or drinks (like 3 juices or 3 kinds of milk), with the labels hidden

lesson.text: A useful review says what you think, gives a reason, and proves it with a detail the reader can picture. The best ones also admit one downside and say whether it was worth it.
lesson.before: The park was good. I liked it. 5 stars.

model.line: Riverside Park is the best park in town for climbing.
It has the biggest climbing structure around.
The rope pyramid is twice as tall as the one at school, and there's a net at the top you can lie in.
The only bad part: the bathrooms were locked.
Totally. It's free, and better than the park we drive to. 4 acorns out of 5.

lesson.modelNote: A stranger had nothing to go on in the first one. The fix adds a reason, a detail you can picture and one honest downside.

howTo.intro: Your one word all week is 'why?'. When something was 'good', ask why, and how a reader would know.

plan.what: The taste test and the rating system (Steps 1 and 2). About 20 minutes.
One review after each outing, meal or book (Steps 3 and 4).
Put the column together and share it (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: Your kid doesn't like writing yet
troubleshoot.a: They say the review out loud and you write it down word for word. They still design the rating.
Read two real reviews together, a helpful one and a useless one. Ask which would help you decide.
Have them rank three things of the same kind first, then score them. Two can't both be the best, and the score has to show the gap.

fromHome.text: At the end of every trip, my kids review the country we just lived in and score it out of 100, ten points per category. Here's a bit of Panama's. We rated every Disney ride the same way.
quotes: Nature and animals, 9/10. The nature and the animals are amazing, but I took off a point because there are too many mosquitoes.
Transport, 10/10. It was always easy to find a ride and the prices were super low. A 15 km taxi ride cost $4.

skills.name: Writing for a reader

steps.title: Run a blind taste test
steps.why: A silly first review that teaches the whole skill, then a list of things to review.
steps.kid: You hide the labels on 3 snacks, cereals or drinks (3 juices, 3 sodas, 3 kinds of milk), and everyone, your kid included, tries each one blind. Your kid rates them and says why: which won, which lost, and what exactly made the difference. Then they make a list of real things they could review this week and pick 3 to 5 they have strong feelings about, good or bad.
steps.you: Set up the taste test and play along. When your kid says 'this one's better,' ask what makes it better until you get something specific, like 'crunchier' or 'less sweet.' Then help them remember what they've eaten, read, played or visited lately, and let them choose.
ask: Which one won, and what exactly made it better?
Is there something everyone loves that you think is overrated?
steps.tip: Pick things they actually love or can't stand. One honest 'skip this' makes a column more believable than five glowing reviews.

levels.explore: Do the taste test and say which one won and why. Pick 2 or 3 things to review.
levels.develop: Rate all three with a reason for each. Pick 3 or 4 things of at least 2 different kinds.
levels.extend: Run it again with the labels showing. Did any score change? Write what the label did to your opinion.

steps.title: Make the rating system
steps.why: Your kid decides how the column scores things, and what each score means.
steps.kid: Your kid invents the rating system they'll use for every review. It can be stars, a number out of 10, or something of their own like acorns or slices of pizza. Older kids can score out of 100 with categories, ten points each, and take points off with a reason. Then they write down what the top and bottom scores mean and test the system on the taste-test winner.
steps.you: Ask the questions that pin it down. What's the difference between a 3 and a 4? Could a stranger understand the score without asking? Let them change it after the test.
ask: What does it take to get your top score?
When you take a point off, can you say exactly why?
steps.tip: Scoring out of 100 by category is what our kids use for every country we visit. Taking points off forces a reason every time.

levels.explore: Draw 1 to 5 stars (or acorns) and say what 1 star and 5 stars mean.
levels.develop: Write a clear meaning for each level, test it on 2 things and adjust it.
levels.extend: Score by category, then decide which category matters most and count it double. Does the winner change?

steps.title: Try it with a reviewer's eye
steps.why: Before writing, your kid tries each thing again and takes notes.
steps.kid: Your kid tries each thing again, this time on purpose: rereads the chapter, goes back to the park, eats the snack slowly. They jot down what they notice, the good and the bad, and anything a reader would want to know first. If it costs money, they find out the price and compare it with something similar.
steps.you: Join them if you can. Ask what they're noticing, not what they think of it yet. If the notes say 'fun' or 'yummy,' ask what exactly made it fun.
ask: What would someone want to know before trying this?
Was it worth the money, or is there something just as good for less?
steps.tip: Notes are details, not opinions. 'The slide gets so hot in the sun' is a note. 'Bad slide' isn't, yet.

levels.explore: Say or draw 3 things you noticed about each one.
levels.develop: Note what was good, what wasn't, and the price if there is one.
levels.extend: Work out cost per use: a $12 book read 3 times costs $4 a read. Compare that with something similar.

steps.title: Write the reviews
steps.why: Your kid turns the notes into reviews, then fixes them for a reader.
steps.kid: Your kid writes each review the way the example at the start does: opinion first, then a reason, proof from their notes, one fair downside, and whether it was worth it, with the rating at the end. Then they read it out loud and swap vague words like 'good,' 'nice' and 'fun' for exact ones.
steps.you: Read each review as if you've never tried the thing. Could you decide from it? Give one suggestion per review, like 'tell me why the pizza was the best,' then let them make the change.
ask: If someone only read your first sentence, would they know your opinion?
Who would love this? Who would hate it? Did you say so?
steps.tip: If a review has no proof, ask 'what would I see if I went?' Whatever they answer is the proof sentence.

levels.explore: Say it first: what it is, what you think, and one 'because'. Then write or dictate it.
levels.develop: Write an opinion, 2 or 3 reasons with proof, one downside, and a rating.
levels.extend: Rewrite one review for a different reader, like a grandparent or a 5-year-old. Which details stay, and which go?

steps.title: Publish the column and share it
steps.why: The reviews become a real column, and someone actually uses it.
steps.kid: Your kid names the column, makes a header, and puts the reviews together with the same format and rating system. Then they share it with at least two people and ask which review was most useful, and whether it made them want to try something or skip it.
steps.you: Help put it together if needed, but let them decide how it looks. Read it like a real reader and tell them which review helped you most, and why. Then talk about whether the column keeps going.
ask: If this were in a newspaper, would someone want to read it?
Did writing the review change your mind about anything?
steps.tip: Tell them who the first reader will be before the final copy. A named reader changes the writing more than any correction.

levels.explore: Name the column, put the reviews in order, and share them with one person.
levels.develop: Add a header and matching format, share with two people, and write down their feedback.
levels.extend: Ask each reader which review they'd trust enough to act on, and what made them trust it. Add that to your weakest review.

conclusion.headline: Their column helps someone else choose.
conclusion.text: Call a café 'good' and stop there. See whether they ask what made it good and what it cost. A reader needs both before they choose, and your kid knows that now.
conclusion.celebrate: When you get to the downside in a review of something they loved, tell them: 'You loved it and still told me the bad part. That's why I'd trust your next review.'
extensions: Keep the column going: one new review after every outing
Review five things of the same kind, like five parks, and make a ranking
Score a family movie night out of 100, by category
Review the same thing as a sibling and compare your scores
Read a real newspaper review together and find its opinion, reason and proof

signs: They give a reason on their own: 'It was good because...'
They notice details in the moment ('I'm putting this in my review')
They start asking what things cost, and whether they're worth it
makeItReal: Hand a finished review to the person it's about: the café owner, the librarian who recommended the book, the park's community board. Let your kid watch them read it, then write the next review with that reader in mind.

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.
